claims.text: Thermal exposure of a metastable Mg-containing lightweight HEA causes diffusion-driven precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
The precipitated compounds may include Mg2X or MgX phases, where X can be Al or Zn.
Mg-rich intermetallics nucleate preferentially at grain boundaries and triple junctions.
Increasing temperature accelerates the proposed precipitation pathway.
Intermetallic precipitation depletes Mg from the alloy matrix.
Mg depletion and formation of galvanically active intermetallics reduce corrosion resistance.
Mg depletion and intermetallic formation reduce high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The initial as-cast or rapidly solidified state has minimal intermetallic content and a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Thermally activated diffusion breaks down local supersaturation and produces intermetallic precipitation.
Intermetallic formation disrupts solid-solution strengthening.
Intermetallic formation alters the local electrochemical environment and promotes micro-galvanic corrosion.
The evolved phases reduce the protective character of oxide scales.
Annealing will increase the volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallics, particularly at grain boundaries, relative to the initial state.
Annealing will measurably reduce the Mg concentration of the matrix relative to the initial state.
Annealing will increase oxidation mass gain and corrosion current density relative to the initial state.
Intermetallic formation may embrittle the alloy.
The initial homogeneous solid-solution state has high corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Below approximately 300°C, diffusion is too slow to cause significant intermetallic precipitation within service times.
Below approximately 300°C, the metastable solid solution and its associated corrosion and oxidation properties are retained.
The kinetics and morphology of intermetallic formation vary with alloy composition and processing history.
